**Answer**

According to Elections Canada, **Quebec** had more valid votes under special voting rules when all five federal elections (40th – 2008, 41st – 2011, 42nd – 2015, 43rd – 2019, 44th – 2021) are summed together.

| Election | Quebec (valid votes) | British Columbia (valid votes) |
|----------|-----------------------|--------------------------------|
| 2008 (40th) | 65,394 | 34,475 |
| 2011 (41st) | 66,514 | 37,890 |
| 2015 (42nd) | 128,053 | 101,781 |
| 2019 (43rd) | 124,750 | 101,121 |
| 2021 (44th) | 166,657 | 216,240 |
| **Total** | **551,368** | **491,507** |

**Sources**

- 2008 – Table 6 “Distribution of valid votes under Special Voting Rules”: Quebec 65,394; BC 34,475【source 8】.
- 2011 – Table 6: Quebec 66,514; BC 37,890【source 9】.
- 2015 – Table 6: Quebec 128,053; BC 101,781【source 10】.
- 2019 – Table 6: Quebec 124,750; BC 101,121【source 11】.
- 2021 – Table 6: Quebec 166,657; BC 216,240【source 11】.

Adding the figures for each province shows Quebec’s total (551,368) exceeds British Columbia’s total (491,507). Therefore, Quebec had more valid votes under special voting rules across the five elections.

This page provides data on the number of special ballot voting kits Elections Canada issued to electors, both in Canada and abroad, during the 2021 federal election. Special ballots are used when an elector votes by mail, or when they vote in person at a local Elections Canada office.
For these electors, the deadline to apply to vote by special ballot in the 2021 general election was Tuesday, September 14, 6 p.m. Electors had to return their completed special ballots by election day, Monday, September 20. Special ballots received after the election day deadlines are not counted.
Special ballots are also used by incarcerated electors voting at their correctional facility, and by certain Canadian Forces electors.
More detail on the special ballot voting process, and on special ballot voting data from the 2021 federal election is available in our report: A Special Ballot Report – 44th General Election. That report refers to 'outer envelopes', which is the portion of the voting kit that electors return when they vote. Electors place their completed ballot into an unmarked 'inner' envelope, which is then inserted into the outer envelope to be returned. While this webpage refers to 'voting kits', this term is interchangeable with the 'outer envelopes' referred to in the report.

Title: Context - Special Ballot Report – 45th General Election
Chunks: 0
In recent elections, there has been an increase in the number of electors voting within their electoral district (local electors) using the special ballot process, whether by mail or at their local Elections Canada office (the office of the returning officer for the electoral district). Special ballots for these electors are issued and counted at the local office.
There has also been a rise over time in the use of special ballots to provide greater access to voting services and flexibility to electors in various situations.
During the 44th general election in 2021, which took place during the COVID-19 pandemic, 507,772 local electors voted by mail, a significant increase relative to previous elections. In the 45th general election, this number fell to 140,885, a decrease of 72%.
Special ballots are used to serve electors, whether inside or outside their electoral district, who are:
*   incarcerated  
*   homebound (if certain criteria are met)  
*   members of the Canadian Armed Forces  
*   students  
*   living overseas  
*   living in remote and Indigenous communities  
*   working in isolated locations  
*   unable to access standard voting services due to a weather-related event or natural disaster  
*   residing in a long-term care facility without a mobile poll  
*   receiving care in an acute care facility
The flexibility of the special ballot enables Elections Canada to offer voting options to electors who are outside their electoral district or otherwise unable to get to their assigned polling station. However, special ballot voting comes with some challenges from the election administrator’s perspective, especially as the use of special ballots increases. These challenges include, but are not limited to, postal delivery service standards or delays, the special ballot’s lack of accessibility features, procedural complexities and legislated deadlines.

The report provides an overview of the activities carried out by the Office of the Commissioner of Canada Elections (OCCE) between April 1, 2025, and March 31, 2026, in relation to compliance and enforcement activities under the _Canada Elections Act_ (the Act).
The 2025–2026 fiscal year was marked by the 45th federal general election, a pivotal moment for the OCCE. The annual report includes an analysis of the complaints most frequently received during the election period.

_-- Caroline J. Simard_

# The 40th Canadian General Election in Perspective
## The 40th Canadian General Election in Perspective
The Public Policy Forum hosts an event entitled "The Morning After: The 40th Canadian General Election in Perspective," Ottawa, Ont., October 16, 2008.
In this post-election event, participants examine and discuss the results of the 2008 federal election. The panellists are David Emerson (Minister of Foreign Affairs), Peter Donolo (partner, Strategic Council), Joël-Denis Bellavance (Ottawa Bureau chief for La Presse), and Michel Dorais (former comissioner, Canada Revenue Agency).
After speaking, panellists field questions from forum attendees.

Title: Context - Special Ballot Report – 45th General Election
Chunks: 0,7,8,9,10
In recent elections, there has been an increase in the number of electors voting within their electoral district (local electors) using the special ballot process, whether by mail or at their local Elections Canada office (the office of the returning officer for the electoral district). Special ballots for these electors are issued and counted at the local office.
There has also been a rise over time in the use of special ballots to provide greater access to voting services and flexibility to electors in various situations.
During the 44th general election in 2021, which took place during the COVID-19 pandemic, 507,772 local electors voted by mail, a significant increase relative to previous elections. In the 45th general election, this number fell to 140,885, a decrease of 72%.
Special ballots are used to serve electors, whether inside or outside their electoral district, who are:
*   incarcerated  
*   homebound (if certain criteria are met)  
*   members of the Canadian Armed Forces  
*   students  
*   living overseas  
*   living in remote and Indigenous communities  
*   working in isolated locations  
*   unable to access standard voting services due to a weather-related event or natural disaster  
*   residing in a long-term care facility without a mobile poll  
*   receiving care in an acute care facility
The flexibility of the special ballot enables Elections Canada to offer voting options to electors who are outside their electoral district or otherwise unable to get to their assigned polling station. However, special ballot voting comes with some challenges from the election administrator’s perspective, especially as the use of special ballots increases. These challenges include, but are not limited to, postal delivery service standards or delays, the special ballot’s lack of accessibility features, procedural complexities and legislated deadlines.

## Administrative Count of Special Ballots in Coquitlam–Port Coquitlam, Northumberland–Clarke and Cape Breton–Canso–Antigonish
The votes in all impacted electoral districts had been validly cast and should normally have been counted. Because of this, the Chief Electoral Officer ordered an administrative count of these ballots following validation of the election results. Although the votes cannot be included in the official results, for the sake of transparency and to reflect all legally cast ballots, the tallies will be published alongside the Official Voting Results, except in instances where the secrecy of the vote could not be protected.
Appendix B provides a detailed breakdown of the results of the administrative counts, except where the secrecy of the vote may be compromised.

## Local Elections Canada Offices
969,964 special ballot voting kits issued
5%Fewer than in the 2021 federal election
924,598 valid votes
10,108 received late and set aside in accordance with the Canada Elections Act
35,258 not returned

## Office of the Chief Electoral Officer
402,763 special ballot voting kits issued
55%More than in the 2021 federal election
325,173 valid votes
34,594 set aside in accordance with the Canada Elections Act
42,996 not returned

## Footnotes
Return to footnote 1 Slightly different rules apply to incarcerated electors and to Canadian Armed Forces members voting at military polls.
Return to footnote 2 As of July 7, 2025. This value is adjusted upward in the months following the election as late ballots continue to arrive at the OCEO.
Return to footnote 3 As of July 7, 2025. This value is adjusted downward in the months following the election as late ballots continue to arrive at the OCEO.
Return to footnote 4 An administrative count revealed that 821 national special ballots had been mistakenly kept at the local Elections Canada office. The original figure of 822 was a transcription error.
Return to footnote 5 National special ballots are ballots cast by electors who live in Canada but are outside their electoral district.
Return to footnote 6 Owing to differences between federal and provincial election laws, staff at the local Elections Canada office misunderstood the Special Voting Rules. Office staff discovered their error three days after election day when, having received no instructions on what to do with the national special ballots, which should not be counted at local offices, they reviewed the guidelines. They promptly notified Elections Canada of the mistake.
Return to footnote 7 Local special ballots are ballots cast by electors from within their electoral district.

# Report on Special Polling Measures
26 may 2022
Categories:General election, Municipal
We are posting a new document on our website today: the _Report on Special Polling Measures – 2021 Municipal General Elections_(in French only).
Produced thanks to the collaboration of returning officers in Québec municipalities following the 2021 municipal general elections, this report describes the main measures taken to adapt the _Act respecting elections and referendums in municipalities_:
1.   Extension of the election period  
2.   Additional voting days  
3.   Extended and standardized voting times  
4.   Use of voters’ own pencils  
5.   Counting of advance poll ballots beginning at 6 p.m.  
6.   Identity verification panel at the polling stations  
7.   Health protocol
The report outlines the returning officers’ satisfaction with each measure, how they implemented them, and any problems or difficulties they encountered.
Certain measures may be proposed as legislative amendments to ensure they are used on a permanent basis, as part of the municipal election process update.
Voting by mail extension is addressed in a separate report (PDF – in French), given the significance and scope of this particular measure.
We would like to extend our sincere thanks to the returning officers for their feedback and efforts to ensure that their elections always run smoothly, regardless of the context.
Read the full Report on Special Polling Measures (PDF – in French) for more information.
The _Charter of the French language_ and its regulations govern the consultation of English-language content.

# Report on Special Polling Measures
26 may 2022
Categories:General election, Municipal
We are posting a new document on our website today: the _Report on Special Polling Measures – 2021 Municipal General Elections_(in French only).
Produced thanks to the collaboration of returning officers in Québec municipalities following the 2021 municipal general elections, this report describes the main measures taken to adapt the _Act respecting elections and referendums in municipalities_:
1.   Extension of the election period  
2.   Additional voting days  
3.   Extended and standardized voting times  
4.   Use of voters’ own pencils  
5.   Counting of advance poll ballots beginning at 6 p.m.  
6.   Identity verification panel at the polling stations  
7.   Health protocol
The report outlines the returning officers’ satisfaction with each measure, how they implemented them, and any problems or difficulties they encountered.
Certain measures may be proposed as legislative amendments to ensure they are used on a permanent basis, as part of the municipal election process update.
Voting by mail extension is addressed in a separate report (PDF – in French), given the significance and scope of this particular measure.
We would like to extend our sincere thanks to the returning officers for their feedback and efforts to ensure that their elections always run smoothly, regardless of the context.

According to Elections Canada, **Quebec** had more valid votes under special voting rules when all five federal elections (40th – 2008, 41st – 2011, 42nd – 2015, 43rd – 2019, 44th – 2021) are summed together.

| Election | Quebec (valid votes) | British Columbia (valid votes) |

- 2011 – Table 6: Quebec 66,514; BC 37,890【source 9】.
- 2015 – Table 6: Quebec 128,053; BC 101,781【source 10】.
- 2019 – Table 6: Quebec 124,750; BC 101,121【source 11】.
- 2021 – Table 6: Quebec 166,657; BC 216,240【source 11】.
